content.title: About
content.content: Injera is a traditional Ethiopian flatbread made from a fermented batter of whole‑grain teff. The batter is left to sour for several days, giving the bread a mildly tangy flavor and a spongy, elastic texture that can be torn and used as both plate and utensil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Teff is the only grain almost exclusively cultivated in Ethiopia and Eritrea; it thrives in drought‑prone, low‑nutrient soils.
Injera is traditionally served as a large sheet on which various stews (wat) and vegetables are placed; diners tear pieces with their hands.
Fermentation lasts 2–5 days, during which beneficial bacteria develop, enhancing digestibility.
There are more than 30 regional varieties of injera, differing in thickness, color, and aroma.
Using injera as a plate reduces the amount of dishware needed for a meal.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: The natural fermentation of teff promotes growth of beneficial microbes that support gut health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Injera raises blood sugar slowly, making it suitable for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Teff provides substantial dietary fiber, aiding regular digestion.

items.title: Contains iron and calcium
items.content: Teff is a notable source of iron, calcium, and magnesium, essential for bone and blood health.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Because teff is naturally gluten‑free, injera is safe for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Teff allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to teff, ranging from skin rashes to digestive upset.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Teff contains phytates, which can inhibit mineral absorption if consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Sodium in accompaniments
items.content: Injera is often served with salty sauces; people limiting sodium should watch portion sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Injera is used as a base for stews (wat), vegetable and meat dishes, and as a “spoon” to scoop up sauce. It can be cut into strips, rolled with fillings, or simply eaten as bread alongside butter or honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep injera in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2–3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to a week) or freeze, reheating in the oven before serving.
